subject: Archaeology
title: Cahokia: America's Forgotten City
description: A micro-lesson that makes Cahokia: America's Forgotten City usable.

hook.text: Before Columbus, a city near modern St. Louis had a larger population than London in the year 1100.

buildup.text: Cahokia was home to 20,000 people, with plazas, neighborhoods, and a 100-foot earthen pyramid.

discovery.text: Monks Mound is the largest earthwork in the Americas — bigger at its base than the Great Pyramid of Giza.

twist.text: The city collapsed by 1400. Floods, deforestation, and political unrest likely caused the decline.

climax.text: For centuries, European settlers refused to believe Native Americans built it. They invented lost-race myths.

punchline.text: America's greatest ancient city was ignored because of racism.

quiz.question: What was Monks Mound at Cahokia?
options: A natural hill that the city was built around
The largest earthwork in the Americas, bigger at its base than the Great Pyramid
A burial site containing thousands of artifacts

details.summary: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was the largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, with a population of up to 20,000 at its peak around 1100 CE. Its central Monks Mound is the largest earthen structure in the Americas, yet the city is largely unknown to the American public.
details.whyItMatters: Cahokia challenges the narrative that complex urban civilization in North America began only with European colonization. This indigenous metropolis rivaled contemporary European cities in size and demonstrates pre-Columbian urban sophistication.
takeaways: The largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, peaking around 1100 CE
Monks Mound is the largest earthen structure in the Americas
Challenges narratives that North America lacked urban civilization

faq.question: Why is Cahokia so little known compared to other ancient cities?
faq.answer: As an earthen-mound site rather than stone, Cahokia lacks the visual drama of pyramids or temples. Centuries of farming and suburban development destroyed much of the site. American education traditionally focuses on post-contact history, marginalizing pre-Columbian indigenous achievements.

faq.question: What happened to Cahokia's population?
faq.answer: The city declined rapidly after 1200 CE due to a combination of environmental degradation, political instability, flooding, and possibly disease. By 1400 CE it was abandoned. Descendant communities — possibly including the Osage and other Siouan-speaking peoples — dispersed across the region.
